newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Bank of Taiwan raises prime rate to 7.15 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Taiwan raises prime rate to 7.15 pct.

text.p: The state-owned Bank of Taiwan, the island's biggest commercial bank, said on Wednesday it was raising its prime lending rate by 0.125 percentage point to 7.150 percent, effective Thursday.
The move came nearly a week after the central bank's decision to increase two key interest rates to stabilise the foreign exchange market.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said on July 31 the bank was raising the rediscount rate and accommodations against secured loans to 5.25 and 5.625 percent, respectively, effective August 1.
The state bank also said it was raising its rate on one-to-three-year time deposits by 0.125 percentage point, effective Thursday.

Central bank business director Lee Sheng-yen told reporters after the close of money market trading that the central bank would not force other banks to raise their interest rates, but indicated the Bank of Taiwan move was welcome.
The Bank of Taiwan's rate cut "lived up to the expectations" of the central bank, Lee said.
Other state and private banks were expected to follow the Bank of Taiwan's move and hike their rates.

Central bank officials have said the two central bank rates were raised to ensure stability in the foreign exchange market, where the Taiwan dollar underwent a depreciation of more than four percent since late July.

Market analysts, however, say the central bank also is keen to cool huge turnover in the stock market, where the index has soared through much of 1997 on turnover that has spiked on some days to nearly T$300 billion (US$10.5 billion).
